accept: yeast starter
the starter mash

exp: Kimoto, yamahai and sokujō are the three ways to build it.

q: What is the typical alcohol of undiluted sake before water addition?
exp: Around 18–20%, usually cut to ~15–16% unless sold as genshu — the highest natural fermentation in the beverage world.

hyogo niigata kyoto

seasonal autumn sake

q: Standard sake is pasteurised twice. Name the two part-pasteurised categories and say which hi-ire each one skips.
accept: namachozo skips the first hi-ire namazume skips the second
namachozo is stored raw and pasteurized at bottling namazume is pasteurized before storage and bottled raw
namachozo raw storage namazume raw bottling
one pasteurization each namachozo at bottling namazume before storage
ans: Namachozo: stored raw and given its only pasteurisation at bottling (it skips the first hi-ire). Namazume: pasteurised once before storage and then bottled raw (it skips the second).
exp: The two hi-ire (around 60-65 C) deactivate residual koji enzymes and kill hiochi lactic bacteria, which can spoil sake in the bottle. Skipping one buys freshness and costs stability, so both styles want the cold chain; only a fully raw nama (honnama) skips both. Knowing which step was skipped tells you whether the freshness sits in the storage character or in the bottling.

q: What are honjozo's two numerical limits - polishing, and alcohol addition?
accept: seimaibuai of 70 or lower and alcohol capped at 10 percent of the white rice weight
polished to 70% with brewer's alcohol limited to 10% of the polished rice
70% seimaibuai and a 10% alcohol addition limit
at most 70 percent seimaibuai and at most 10 percent added alcohol by weight of the polished rice
ans: Rice polished to a seimaibuai of 70% or lower, and added distilled alcohol capped at 10% of the weight of the white (polished) rice used. Koji rice must also be at least 15% of the total rice, as in every tokutei meishoshu grade.
exp: The cap is what separates honjozo from futsushu, which is bound by no such limit and may also carry added sugars and acids. At honjozo's scale the alcohol is not padding: distilled spirit pulls aroma compounds out of the mash and dries the finish, which is why honjozo is the classic warming sake. Tokubetsu Honjozo needs 60% or lower, or a declared special method.

q: Under the National Tax Agency's current labelling standards, a sake may be called junmai-shu if it meets which requirement?
opts: At least 40% of the grain polished away, alcohol allowed
No added alcohol and at least 30% koji rice by weight
No added distilled alcohol, with no minimum polishing ratio
No added alcohol and at least 30% of the grain polished off
exp: The 70% ceiling on junmai was abolished effective 2004 - option 4 states the rule as it stood before that. What remains is the absence of added distilled alcohol, koji rice of at least 15% (not 30%), and a seimaibuai declared on the label. So a junmai polished to only 80% is perfectly legal, and several respected breweries make one. The 60% figure reappears only at Tokubetsu Junmai. Follow the standard, not the older textbooks.

q: Define kasu-buai and say what a high figure tells you about the sake.
accept: the pressed lees as a percentage of rice used higher means more of the mash was discarded
kasu buai is the sake lees ratio and it runs high for daiginjo
lees percentage against rice weight gentle pressing and a selective cut raise it
sake lees left after pressing expressed as a share of the rice
ans: Kasu is the pressed lees cake; kasu-buai is its weight expressed as a percentage of the rice used. Around 20-25% is ordinary for a junmai, while a competition daiginjo can leave 40-50% behind. A high figure means gentle pressing and a selective cut - more of the mash thrown away in pursuit of a cleaner wine.
exp: This is one of the honest explanations for daiginjo's price: the brewer is paying for rice that never reaches the bottle. Nothing is wasted commercially - kasu is sold for kasuzuke pickles, amazake and cooking - but the yield loss is real. Compare it with fukuro-zuri drip lots, where kasu-buai climbs higher still.
